meta.title: Cardiac Muscle
meta.summary: Cardiac muscle borrows skeletal muscle's machinery but solves a completely different problem: it must beat, on its own, without stopping, for a lifetime.

items: Cardiac muscle borrows skeletal muscle's machinery but solves a completely different problem: it must beat, on its own, without stopping, for a lifetime.
Three design changes make that possible — it generates its own rhythm, its cells are electrically joined into one team, and it physically cannot cramp.
Everything in this topic is the heart answering one question: how do you build a pump that never gets a day off and never seizes up?
Keep skeletal muscle in mind throughout — the differences are the lesson.
Striated like skeletal muscle (same sarcomeres), but the cells are short, branched, and usually have one nucleus.
Involuntary — you cannot decide to beat. Nerves only adjust a rhythm the heart already produces itself.
Packed with mitochondria (a far higher proportion than skeletal muscle), because it can never afford to run out of energy or work anaerobically for long.

Intercalated discs are the signature feature — specialised junctions joining cell to cell, containing desmosomes (mechanical rivets that stop cells tearing apart) and gap junctions (electrical tunnels).
Those gap junctions are why the heart behaves as a functional syncytium: excite one cell and the whole chamber contracts together.
A transplanted heart has no nerve supply — and still beats. It proves the rhythm is built into the muscle, not sent from the brain.
The heart's dependence on oxygen is why a blocked coronary artery causes damage within minutes: this muscle cannot function anaerobically for long.

blocks.x: Skeletal muscle gets to rest between contractions. Cardiac muscle doesn't have that luxury — it must contract roughly once a second, every second, for an entire lifetime, without you ever consciously telling it to. This section explains how it's built and wired to make that possible.
▶️Structure of the Cardiac MuscleVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle (definition)
blocks.def: A type of involuntary striated muscle found within the heart. Its function is to 'pump' blood through the circulatory system.

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle cell shape and arrangement
blocks.def: Branched, interlacing striated cells — unlike the long, straight, unbranched fibers of skeletal muscle, cardiac cells branch and interconnect with their neighbors.

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle striations vs skeletal
blocks.def: The cross-striations in cardiac muscle are LESS distinct than in skeletal muscle, though the same basic <term d="The basic contracting unit of a muscle fibre, running from one Z-line to the next.">sarcomere</term> organization is present.

blocks.name: Nervous control of cardiac muscle
blocks.def: Innervated by the autonomic nervous system — this is involuntary control, quite different from skeletal muscle's voluntary control by somatic motor neurons.

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle nuclei
blocks.def: Predominantly MONOnucleate (one nucleus per cell) — a key structural difference from skeletal muscle's multinucleated fibers.

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle mitochondria
blocks.def: Numerous, large, and well-developed mitochondria — reflecting cardiac muscle's total reliance on continuous aerobic (oxidative) metabolism; it cannot afford to 'run out of gas' the way skeletal muscle sometimes can.

blocks.name: Cardiac myocyte size
blocks.def: Narrower and much SHORTER than skeletal muscle cells.

blocks.title: Next up — the junctions that make the heart one unit

items: This is the single biggest structural difference from skeletal muscle, so read it carefully.
Desmosomes = mechanical rivets, stopping cells from tearing apart under a lifetime of pulling.
Gap junctions = electrical tunnels, letting the impulse pass straight from cell to cell.
Together they make the heart a functional syncytium — many cells behaving as one.

blocks.name: Intercalated discs
blocks.def: The specialized junctions that join cardiac muscle cells to one another. They contain gap junctions, which allow electrical signals (ions) to pass directly from one cell's cytoplasm into the next.

blocks.name: Desmosomes (in cardiac muscle)
blocks.def: Mechanically link adjacent cardiac cells together at the intercalated discs, providing the physical strength to withstand the constant mechanical stress of contraction without cells tearing apart.

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle as a <term d="A group of cells joined so closely that they respond electrically as a single unit.">syncytium</term>
blocks.def: Because cardiac cells are electrically coupled via gap junctions at intercalated discs, the whole heart (or at least each chamber) behaves as a single electrical unit, a 'syncytium' — an electrical signal starting in one cell spreads to ALL connected cells, letting the heart contract as one coordinated whole rather than as thousands of independent cells.

blocks.name: Sarcomeres in cardiac muscle
blocks.def: Cardiac muscle has <term d="The thin filament protein that the thick filaments grab and pull on during contraction.">actin</term> and <term d="The thick filament protein whose heads pull on actin to shorten the muscle.">myosin</term> microfilaments organized into sarcomeres, just like skeletal muscle — the same fundamental contractile unit, reused.

blocks.title: Next up — small differences with big consequences

items: Cardiac T-tubules are larger but fewer, and pair with just one cistern — a diad, not a triad.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum is less developed than in skeletal muscle, storing less calcium.
That shortfall is exactly why the heart must borrow calcium from outside the cell — the basis of calcium-induced calcium release.

blocks.name: T-tubules in cardiac muscle vs skeletal
blocks.def: Typically WIDER than in skeletal muscle. There is only ONE T-tubule per sarcomere (located close to the Z-line), compared to skeletal muscle's arrangement of two T-tubules per sarcomere.

blocks.name: Diads (in cardiac muscle)
blocks.def: The structure formed where a cardiac T-tubule associates with just a SINGLE terminal cistern of <term d="The muscle cell's internal calcium store, released to trigger contraction.">sarcoplasmic reticulum</term> — contrast this with skeletal muscle's 'triads,' where one T-tubule is flanked by TWO terminal cisternae.

blocks.name: Sarcoplasmic reticulum in cardiac muscle
blocks.def: Much LESS developed than in skeletal muscle fibers — this matters, because it means cardiac muscle relies more heavily on calcium entering from OUTSIDE the cell to trigger contraction, rather than solely on internally stored calcium.

items: Two different action potentials live in one organ: fast-response (working muscle of the atria and ventricles) and slow-response (pacemaker tissue).
Working cells wait to be told. Pacemaker cells tell.

blocks.x: Cardiac muscle has two completely different 'personalities' of electrical behavior depending on where in the heart you look: most of the heart muscle fires a sharp, fast action potential only when told to — but a special group of cells generates its OWN rhythm, spontaneously, over and over, forever. That second group is what makes your heart a self-starting pump.
▶️Action Potential in Cardiac MuscleVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: <term d="The difference in electrical charge between the inside and outside of a cell membrane.">Resting membrane potentialThe steady negative charge inside a cell while it is not firing.</term> of cardiac muscle
blocks.def: About -90 mV for individual (non-pacemaker) cardiac muscle cells — similar in magnitude to a resting neuron.

blocks.name: Two general types of cardiac action potentials
blocks.def: Non-pacemaker action potentials ('fast response') and pacemaker potentials ('slow response') — the working heart muscle uses one type, the specialized rhythm-generating tissue uses the other.

sections.title: The Non-Pacemaker (Fast Response) Action Potential — 5 Phases

items: The famous difference from a nerve spike is the plateau (phase 2) — calcium entering balances potassium leaving, holding the cell depolarized.
That plateau stretches the action potential to a few hundred milliseconds, instead of the millisecond or two in a neuron.
Phase 3 is final repolarization (calcium channels shut, potassium exit wins); phase 4 is the stable resting potential.
The plateau is not a quirk — it is the whole safety mechanism, because it keeps the cell refractory until contraction is nearly over.
Many heart drugs are named for exactly this: calcium-channel blockers act on the plateau, which is why they slow the heart and relax vessels.

blocks.cap: The 5 phases of a non-pacemaker cardiac action potential, including the plateau.

blocks.name: Phase 0 (rapid <term d="A shift of the membrane potential toward zero — the inside of the cell becomes less negative.">depolarization</term>)
blocks.def: Due to the opening of fast Na+ channels, causing a rapid increase in Na+ conductance (gNa) and a rapid influx of Na+ (INa) into the cell. Simultaneously, gK+ and outward K+ currents FALL as potassium channels close. Together, these two changes move the membrane potential away from EK and toward ENa (the sodium equilibrium potential) — an extremely fast upstroke.

blocks.name: Phase 1 (initial <term d="The return of the membrane potential back to its resting negative value after firing.">repolarization</term>)
blocks.def: Occurs with inactivation of the fast Na+ channels, repulsion of further Na+ entry (since the interior is now positive), a transient net outward K+ current, and Cl- efflux — together producing a brief, small dip in voltage right after the peak.

blocks.name: Phase 2 (the plateau)
blocks.def: The distinctive 'plateau' phase of the cardiac action potential — sustained by a BALANCE between inward movement of Ca2+ (ICa, through L-type Ca2+ channels) and outward movement of K+ (through the slow delayed rectifier K+ channels, IKs). This plateau is what makes the cardiac action potential last far longer than a neuron's — and that extended duration is exactly what prevents the heart from being tetanized (see Mechanical Properties below).

blocks.name: Phase 3 (final repolarization)
blocks.def: The L-type Ca2+ channels close; the slow delayed rectifier (IKs) K+ channels remain open; rapid delayed rectifier K+ channels (IKr) and the inwardly rectifying K+ current (IK1) also open. The resulting net outward, positive current repolarizes the cell back toward resting potential.

blocks.name: Phase 4 (resting membrane potential)
blocks.def: The delayed rectifier K+ channels close once membrane potential is restored to about -80 to -85 mV; IK1 remains conducting throughout phase 4, helping set the resting membrane potential. The Na+-K+ pump restores the ionic concentration gradients, exchanging Na+ for K+ in a 3:2 ratio.

sections.title: Pacemaker Tissue — The Heart's Own Built-In Rhythm Section

items: Pacemaker cells have no stable resting potential. They drift upward on their own until they hit threshold and fire — then do it again, forever.
That drift is phase 4, the 'prepotential', and it is the reason the heart is automatic.
Only three phases here (4, 0, 3) — no plateau, and phase 0 is driven by calcium rather than sodium, which is why it rises more slowly.
The SA node drifts fastest, so it fires first and sets the pace for everyone — the fastest pacemaker wins.
The conduction system then distributes that beat in order: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
It is a drummer setting tempo for a band — everyone could keep time, but they follow whoever counts fastest.
If the SA node fails, a slower pacemaker downstream takes over: the heart keeps beating, just more slowly — the basis of several rhythm disorders and of artificial pacemakers.

blocks.name: Pacemaker tissue (definition)
blocks.def: Tissues that govern the rhythmic occurrence of the heartbeat. These cells have NO true resting potential — they exhibit automaticity, meaning they generate regular, spontaneous action potentials all on their own, with no external trigger needed.

blocks.cap: The 3-phase pacemaker potential — no true resting phase, just endless spontaneous cycling.

blocks.name: The cardiac conduction system
blocks.def: Constituted by the pacemaker cells, including the sinoatrial (SA) node, atrial internodal pathways, atrioventricular (AV) node, Bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers — this is the wiring that carries and coordinates the spontaneous rhythm through the whole heart.

blocks.name: Sinoatrial (SA) node
blocks.def: In the human heart, the cardiac rhythm normally takes its ORIGIN here — it is the heart's natural, dominant pacemaker.

blocks.name: Pacemaker action potential — three phases (not five)
blocks.def: Unlike the working (non-pacemaker) cardiac cell's 5 phases, the pacemaker action potential has only three: Phase 4 (spontaneous depolarization), Phase 0 (depolarization), and Phase 3 (repolarization) — there is no true resting phase and no distinct plateau.

blocks.name: Phase 4 of the pacemaker potential (the 'prepotential')
blocks.def: The spontaneous, slow depolarization phase that gives pacemaker cells their automaticity. Caused by: a continuous outward 'leak' of K+ through K+ channels setting the resting potential (-60 to -70 mV); DECREASING K+ conductance, which partly initiates the slow depolarization; a slow inward flow of Na+ called the 'funny current' (activated by <term d="When the inside of the cell becomes even more negative than its normal resting value.">hyperpolarization</term>); and an inward flow of Ca2+ through T-type Ca2+ channels. This slow depolarization continues until <term d="The minimum strength of stimulus needed to trigger an action potential.">threshold</term> (-40 to -50 mV) is reached, at which point the cell enters Phase 0.

blocks.name: Phase 0 of the pacemaker potential
blocks.def: The depolarization phase — driven by an INCREASE in Ca2+ conductance and an inward Ca2+ current, flowing through L-type Ca2+ channels. Notice this is fundamentally different from the non-pacemaker Phase 0, which is driven by Na+, not Ca2+.

blocks.name: Phase 3 of the pacemaker potential (repolarization)
blocks.def: Ca2+ channels rapidly inactivate soon after opening; Na+ permeability decreases; K+ conductance increases. Once the cell is fully repolarized (about -60 mV), the entire cycle spontaneously repeats itself, all on its own.

sections.title: Regulating the Pacemaker — Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic

items: The autonomic nervous system does not create the beat — it changes the slope of the drift.
Sympathetic (noradrenaline, β₁ receptors): steeper drift → threshold reached sooner → faster heart rate, plus stronger contraction.
Parasympathetic (vagus, ACh, muscarinic receptors): flatter drift and a more negative start → slower heart rate.
At rest, vagal 'braking' dominates — your heart's intrinsic rate is faster than the rate you actually sit at.
The jolt of your heart pounding when a car nearly hits you is sympathetic drive steepening that slope within a second.
Trained athletes often have resting rates near 45–50 — strong vagal tone holding a naturally faster heart in check.
This section is the ANS (Topic 09) in miniature, acting on one target.

blocks.name: Autonomic regulation of pacemaker activity
blocks.def: The rate of SA nodal firing can be altered by the autonomic nervous system — sympathetic input speeds the heart up, parasympathetic input slows it down.

blocks.name: Sympathetic activation of the SA node
blocks.def: Releases norepinephrine (NE), which INCREASES pacemaker rate by decreasing gK+, enhancing the pacemaker current (If), and increasing slow inward gCa2+ and gNa+. The net effect: it increases the SLOPE of Phase 4, so the pacemaker potential reaches threshold more rapidly, firing action potentials more often — a faster heart rate.

blocks.name: Parasympathetic (vagal) activation of the SA node
blocks.def: Releases acetylcholine (ACh), which DECREASES pacemaker rate by increasing gK+, suppressing the pacemaker current (If), and decreasing slow inward gCa2+ and gNa+ currents. The net effect: it REDUCES the slope of Phase 4, so the pacemaker potential reaches threshold more slowly — a slower heart rate.

items: The end point is identical to skeletal muscle — calcium binds troponin C and the filaments slide. What differs is where the calcium comes from.

Calcium-induced calcium release: a small amount of calcium enters from outside the cell, and that triggers the stores to release much more. Cardiac muscle genuinely needs extracellular calcium; skeletal muscle does not.
Because of that dependence, cardiac force can be graded — more calcium in, stronger beat. Skeletal muscle instead grades force by recruitment and frequency.
Digitalis blocks the sodium pump → sodium builds up → less calcium is pumped out → more calcium inside → stronger contraction.
Relaxation again costs ATP: calcium must be pumped back into stores and out of the cell.
A trickle that opens a floodgate — that is calcium-induced calcium release in one image.
Digitalis (from the foxglove plant) is one of the oldest heart medicines still in use, and its whole action is explained by this one paragraph.

blocks.name: Excitation of the heart
blocks.def: The SA node produces the initial stimulus for contraction. The rest of the myocardium conducts these action potentials via electrical synapses — the gap junctions at intercalated discs. This excitation is modulated throughout by the autonomic nervous system.

blocks.name: <term d="The chain of events linking the electrical signal at the membrane to the actual mechanical contraction.">Excitation-contraction coupling</term> in cardiac muscle
blocks.def: The action potential spreads along the T-tubules, opening dihydropyridine-sensitive (L-type Ca2+) channels in the membrane. The resulting Ca2+ entry stimulates opening of ryanodine-sensitive channels in the (relatively sparse) SR, dumping additional Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm — a process called calcium-induced calcium release.

blocks.x: ▶️Excitation-Contraction Coupling of Cardiac MuscleVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Calcium-induced calcium release
blocks.def: The Ca2+ released from the SR alone is NOT sufficient to fully activate the contractile mechanism in cardiac muscle — it is augmented by additional Ca2+ entry via channels in the general <term d="The cell membrane of a muscle fibre.">sarcolemma</term>, itself triggered by the action potential. This dual-source calcium supply (extracellular entry PLUS SR release) is a defining feature that distinguishes cardiac excitation-contraction coupling from skeletal muscle's, where calcium comes almost entirely from the SR alone.

blocks.name: Final common step: calcium binds troponin C
blocks.def: Just as in skeletal muscle, Ca2+ ultimately couples electrical excitation to contraction by binding troponin C (attached to the actin filament), causing troponin to undergo a conformational change that pulls tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin.

blocks.name: Cardiac contraction tension and calcium
blocks.def: The tension developed by cardiac cells is directly PROPORTIONAL to the intracellular Ca2+ concentration — more calcium available means a stronger contraction, unlike skeletal muscle's more all-or-none twitch behavior at the single-fiber level.

blocks.name: Digitalis (a sodium pump inhibitor)
blocks.def: Increases cardiac contractility by inhibiting the Na+ pump, which leads to accumulation of cytosolic Ca2+ (via reduced Na+/Ca2+ exchange) — a classic pharmacological example that directly demonstrates the calcium-contractility link in cardiac muscle.

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle relaxation
blocks.def: Occurs as Ca2+ is pumped BACK into the SR by a Ca2+-ATPase, and ALSO pumped out to the <term d="All the body fluid sitting outside the cells, including blood plasma and the fluid bathing tissues.">extracellular fluid</term> via a Na+/Ca2+ antiporter and a sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase — cardiac muscle uses both an internal (SR) and external (extracellular) route to clear calcium, unlike skeletal muscle which relies almost exclusively on the SR.

sections.title: Mechanical Properties — Why the Heart Can't Be Tetanized

items: The cardiac action potential is long (that plateau), so its refractory period lasts almost as long as the contraction itself.
By the time the heart can respond to another stimulus, it has already relaxed — so twitches can never summate.
Result: cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized, and this is not a limitation but an absolute requirement.
A pump must alternate — fill, then eject. A permanently contracted heart would fill with nothing and pump nothing.
You have had a calf cramp — a sustained, locked contraction. Imagine that in your heart. The long refractory period is precisely what makes it impossible.
Fibrillation is the closest the heart comes to chaos, and it is deadly for exactly this reason: a heart that quivers instead of alternating pumps no blood.

blocks.name: Cardiac muscle twitch duration
blocks.def: The muscle twitch in cardiac tissue is of almost the SAME duration as the action potential itself — because of that long plateau phase (Phase 2).

blocks.x: ▶️<term d="A short spell straight after firing when the cell cannot fire again, or needs a stronger stimulus.">Refractory Period</term> in Cardiac MuscleVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Why cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized
blocks.def: Because the refractory period extends BEYOND the end of the action potential, cardiac muscle cannot be readily re-stimulated to summate contractions before the previous one is finished — it cannot be tetanized the way skeletal muscle can. This is not a flaw; it is essential: sustained tetanic contraction of the heart would prevent it from ever relaxing to refill with blood, and effective pumping would stop entirely.

items: Same principle as skeletal muscle, with enormous practical consequence: stretch the cardiac fibre more (within limits) and it contracts more forcefully.
Preload = how full the ventricle is before it contracts. More filling → more stretch → stronger beat.
Frank–Starling principle: the heart pumps out what it receives — stroke volume automatically matches venous return.
This is a self-regulating mechanism requiring no nerves at all, which is why a transplanted heart still adjusts its output.
Mechanism: stretch improves filament overlap and increases the myofilaments' sensitivity to calcium.
Stand up quickly, or start walking, and more blood returns to the heart — it beats harder on the very next beat, with no conscious control or nerve signal required.
It also explains the balance between the two sides: whatever the right heart sends to the lungs, the left heart must match, or fluid backs up.

blocks.name: Length as a determinant of cardiac force
blocks.def: Length is a major determinant of how much force cardiac muscle develops. Within limits, an INCREASE in length (<term d="How much the heart muscle is stretched by blood filling it before it contracts.">preload</term>) leads to an increase in active tension AND an increase in the rate of active tension development.

blocks.name: Where cardiac muscle develops maximum tension
blocks.def: Unlike skeletal muscle, the maximum developed tension in cardiac muscle occurs NOT at the resting length, but when the muscle is stretched BEYOND its resting length — cardiac muscle normally operates on the ascending limb of its length-tension curve, so it almost always benefits from more stretch, within physiological limits.

blocks.name: Mechanism linking preload to tension
blocks.def: Changes in active tension caused by changes in preload are related to changes in the NUMBER of actin-myosin crosslinkages formed, and changes in preload ALSO affect active tension by altering the sensitivity of troponin C to calcium — stretching the muscle doesn't just create more overlap, it makes the calcium-sensing machinery itself more responsive.

blocks.name: The Frank-Starling principle
blocks.def: States that the <term d="The volume of blood pushed out by a ventricle in a single beat.">stroke volume</term> of the heart INCREASES in response to an increase in the volume of blood filling the heart (the end-diastolic volume) — this principle is directly based on the length-tension relationship within the ventricle. If end-diastolic volume (preload) increases, ventricular fiber length increases, which increases the muscle's developed tension, which increases the force and volume of the ensuing contraction. This is how the heart automatically matches its output to how much blood returns to it, beat to beat, without needing any outside nervous signal to do so.

sections.title: Cardiac vs Skeletal Muscle — The Key Differences at a Glance

items: Nuclei: skeletal is multinucleated; cardiac usually has one (sometimes two).
Connections: skeletal fibres are electrically separate; cardiac cells are joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions and behave as one unit.
Calcium source: skeletal relies on internal stores alone; cardiac must have extracellular calcium as the trigger.
Control: skeletal is voluntary and needs a nerve to fire at all; cardiac is involuntary and self-exciting.
Action potential length: a few milliseconds in skeletal muscle versus a few hundred in cardiac, because of the plateau.
Tetanus: normal and useful in skeletal muscle; impossible in cardiac muscle — and that impossibility is what keeps you alive.

blocks.x: Physiology exams love asking students to compare cardiac and skeletal muscle directly — here are the differences distilled into quick, memorable contrasts.

blocks.name: Nuclei: cardiac vs skeletal
blocks.def: Cardiac muscle cells are mononucleate (one nucleus); skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated. Memory hook: cardiac cells are 'single-minded.'

blocks.name: Cell connections: cardiac vs skeletal
blocks.def: Cardiac cells are joined by intercalated discs containing gap junctions, letting them act as an electrical syncytium; skeletal muscle fibers are NOT electrically connected to each other at all — each is activated independently by its own <term d="The synapse where a motor nerve meets a muscle fibre.">neuromuscular junction</term>.

blocks.name: Calcium source: cardiac vs skeletal
blocks.def: Skeletal muscle relies almost entirely on calcium released from its well-developed SR. Cardiac muscle has a much less-developed SR and depends on BOTH extracellular calcium entry AND SR release (calcium-induced calcium release) to fully activate contraction.

blocks.name: Control: cardiac vs skeletal
blocks.def: Skeletal muscle is voluntary, controlled by somatic motor neurons, and each contraction requires a fresh nerve signal. Cardiac muscle is involuntary, controlled by the autonomic nervous system, and can generate its OWN rhythm independent of any nerve signal at all (automaticity) — the autonomic nerves only speed it up or slow it down, they don't initiate each beat.

blocks.name: Action potential duration: cardiac vs skeletal/neuron
blocks.def: A skeletal muscle or neuron action potential lasts roughly 1-2 msec. A cardiac (non-pacemaker) action potential lasts 200-400 msec — vastly longer, because of the plateau phase — and this long duration is precisely what makes the long cardiac refractory period, and therefore the impossibility of <term d="A smooth, sustained contraction produced when stimuli arrive too fast for the muscle to relax in between.">tetanus</term>, possible.

blocks.name: Tetanus: cardiac vs skeletal
blocks.def: Skeletal muscle CAN be tetanized (its refractory period is much shorter than its twitch duration, so repeated stimulation summates). Cardiac muscle CANNOT be tetanized (its refractory period outlasts its own twitch), which is a functional necessity, not a limitation — the heart must relax fully between beats to refill with blood.

items: Plateau = calcium in. That single fact explains the long action potential, the long refractory period, and why the heart cannot be tetanized.
Pacemaker cells have no stable resting potential — they drift, and drifting is what makes the heart automatic.
The fastest pacemaker wins — normally the SA node.
Frank–Starling: what comes in goes out. More filling → stronger beat.
Sympathetic = steeper drift = faster; vagal = flatter drift = slower.

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: The heart does not need nerves to beat. Nerves only adjust a rhythm the heart generates itself — a transplanted heart still beats.
Inability to tetanize is a feature, not a weakness. A pump must alternate; a permanently contracted heart would pump nothing.
Preload is about filling, not resistance. Preload = how stretched before contraction; afterload = what it must push against.
Cardiac muscle genuinely needs extracellular calcium; skeletal muscle does not. This is a favourite comparison question.
← Skeletal Muscle (Topic 04): same sarcomere, same sliding filaments, same troponin switch. Learn one machine, then learn what the heart changed and why.
← Excitable Tissues (Topic 03): the plateau and the pacemaker drift are just ion channels opening and closing on a different timetable.
→ Autonomic Nervous System (Topic 09): the sympathetic/parasympathetic tug-of-war on the SA node is a perfect worked example of dual innervation and autonomic tone.
→ Blood & CVS (Topic 08): Frank–Starling is what links this muscle to the circulation it serves.
The one-line summary: a muscle that starts itself, contracts as one, refuses to cramp, and automatically pumps out whatever it is given.

lines: Intrinsic rates in beats per minute for the SA node, the AV node and the Purkinje system — the fastest pacemaker sets the rhythm.

mnemonics.h: The AV delay buys filling time
lines: About a tenth of a second of delay at the AV node lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
The calcium plateau stretches the refractory period across most of contraction, so cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised — it must relax and refill.
Gap junctions in the intercalated discs make the atria act as one syncytium and the ventricles as another, so each contracts all-or-none.
